title: Can randomized O(log log n) LOCAL solvability on trees be decided?
formal: Does there exist an always-terminating Turing algorithm that, given a finite locally checkable labeling specification Π on unrooted bounded-degree trees, decides whether Π admits a randomized LOCAL algorithm using O(1 + log log(n+2)) rounds and producing a globally valid labeling with probability at least 1 − 1/(n+1) on every n-node input? Nodes know the exact n. The implicit constant may depend on Π, but not on n or the input instance.
definitions: A specification consists of integers Δ≥2 and r≥1, finite nonempty input/output alphabets, and a finite list of permitted rooted radius-r neighborhood types. Types record input/output labels, degrees and incident port numbers, but do not mention identifiers or n. All finite nonempty simple unrooted trees of maximum degree Δ, all input labelings, and all port numberings are allowed; a degree-d vertex has ports 1,…,d, independently of ports at the other endpoint. Every node must output one symbol, and the labeling is valid when every node sees a permitted neighborhood. Nodes have distinct identifiers in {1,…,n²}, initially know their own input, ID, ports, degree, Π and n, and use independent private fair random bits. A single finite computable program operates at every node. Communication is synchronous with arbitrary finite messages and unrestricted terminating local computation. The round bound holds for every random tape; the success requirement is joint over the entire labeling, for each fixed input and ID assignment. There is no supplied root, shared random advice, or graph-dependent preprocessing. A specification with an unsolvable instance is a negative instance of the decision problem. Logs have base 2.
answer_criterion: Construct a total decider for this exact property, or prove its undecidability. A classification for one fixed specification, a promise of solvability, or only a test for O(log n) algorithms does not answer the question. This card explicitly specializes the saved full-classification question to one binary threshold; it does not claim this threshold alone decides every complexity class.
context:
A local rulebook describes what a solution should look like near each node. Here a centralized program receives that rulebook and must decide whether random local decisions can coordinate a valid solution within a doubly logarithmic number of communication rounds. It is a question about automatically understanding algorithms, rather than running a particular algorithm on one tree.

On trees under the usual network-size convention, randomness can produce an exponential improvement: sinkless orientation has logarithmic deterministic complexity and doubly logarithmic randomized complexity. Other locally checkable problems remain logarithmic with randomness. Thus the threshold in this card distinguishes real algorithmic behaviors; it is not simply asking whether random bits can be removed.

The known landscape has substantial empty intervals. A gap theorem can tell us that no problem occupies an interval without giving an effective way to determine which side a supplied rulebook occupies. The regular-tree classification paper explicitly marks the gap between randomized doubly logarithmic and logarithmic complexity as having unknown decidability.

The answer required from the decider is only yes or no. On a negative input it need not compute the exact larger complexity, and on a positive input it need not distinguish constant, iterated-logarithmic, and doubly logarithmic algorithms. This avoids hiding an undefined symbolic representation of an arbitrary asymptotic function inside the output requirement.

A small failure probability at one vertex is not the same as a small chance of any error in the network. The statement fixes the latter, and also fixes exact knowledge of n. The 2026 network-size results show that changing this knowledge can change the relationship between randomized and deterministic complexities.
why: Recognizing this threshold would give a general test for fast randomized coordination on branching networks. Undecidability would instead establish a limit on automated classification despite the remarkably sparse list of possible round complexities.

importance.reason: A basic recognition problem at the boundary where randomization yields exponential speedups on trees. It connects local specifications, algorithm synthesis, and effective lower-bound theory.

progress.text: Grunau, Rozhoň, and Brandt establish the complete standard tree complexity landscape, including the randomized doubly logarithmic class; knowing the possible classes does not decide membership.

Balliu and coauthors give polynomial-time classification of the logarithmic-versus-polynomial region in their regular-tree formalism. Figure 1(c) leaves recognition of the randomized O(log log n) threshold open.

Suomela’s updated primary problem list continues to ask for randomized complexity decidability for LCLs with inputs on unrooted trees. This card selects a concrete threshold within that broader request.

Balliu and coauthors show that weakening exact knowledge of n changes the tree landscape and the circumstances in which randomness helps. Those variants are not silently substituted for this card’s model.

Piombi’s discussion still identifies only the polynomial gaps as known decidable for unrooted trees. The new main results concern a logical generalization on rooted trees, rather than the randomized threshold here.
